Description of Paper: Maass et al. (2021) developed a discrete event simulation model for a Mayo Clinic CT department serving emergency, inpatient, and outpatient patients competing for six unique CT machines. Using a real-world case study of ED CT access delays, the researchers tested three operational interventions: adding dedicated patient transporters (1-2 staff), implementing faster creatinine lab testing, and assigning a dedicated nurse to monitor patient readiness. Simulation parameters included arrival rates (varying by patient type, time of day, and day of week), resource capacity (CT machines, transporters, holding bays), processing times (scan duration, image processing, equipment cleaning), patient prioritization rules (trauma/stroke patients highest priority), and resource-activity assignments (matching patients to compatible machines). The results demonstrated that adding one dedicated transporter achieved a 10-minute reduction in ED CT access times and the organization successfully realized these predicted improvements in practice, achieving 80% compliance with their 30-minute access goal and meeting the 25-minute stroke imaging guideline. This case study illustrates how simulation parameters derived from process analysis can be systematically adjusted to achieve specific management objectives in complex healthcare environments with multiple competing patient demands.

Description of Paper: Rezeq et al. (2024) developed a hybrid simulation-optimization approach for relief-aid distribution planning by addressing congestion at security checkpoints in humanitarian supply networks. Using the Kerem Abu Salem checkpoint between Israel and Gaza as a real-world case study, the researchers applied business process reengineering (BPR) to redesign the current security checkpoint process. The results demonstrated that Scenario 6 (combining all redesign improvements including electronic queue management, IT-based document processing, portable scanning equipment, extended working hours, and increased staffing) achieved a 90% reduction in security checkpoint cycle time and 28% reduction in distribution costs compared to the AS-IS model. This case study illustrates how simulation parameters (staffing levels, process times, resource allocation) derived from process reengineering can be systematically translated into quantifiable performance metrics and incorporated into optimization models to achieve specific management objectives in complex, congestion-prone environments.

Description of Paper: Zeinali et al. (2015) developed a simulation-based metamodeling approach for resource planning in emergency departments. The study created a discrete event simulation model of an Iranian hospital's emergency department, then built metamodels to approximate the relationship between simulation inputs (number of receptionists, nurses, residents, and beds) and outputs (total patient waiting time). By testing multiple resource configurations via simulation and using metamodels to efficiently explore the solution space, they identified that reducing nurses from 3 to 2 and adding one resident—while maintaining budget constraints—achieved a 48% reduction in average patient waiting times (from 44 to 23 minutes).

Description of Paper: Mahendra et al. (2024) evaluated and improved the Electronic Traffic Law Enforcement (ETLE) business process at an Indonesian Regional Police Traffic Directorate. They interviewed officers to assess capability levels, revealing a gap between current (Level 2) and target (Level 3) capability. In the improvement phase, they identified that insufficient computer resources and inflexible validation procedures were key bottlenecks limiting validation productivity. They developed seven improvement scenarios: Improvement I (resource adjustment: adding computers and extending work hours) achieved 200.42% productivity increase with 6.94% validation rate; Improvement II (resource adjustment plus allowing same-day validation) achieved 424.74% productivity increase with 12.1% validation rate. This study demonstrates how simulation parameters (staffing, computer availability, working hours, validation period rules) directly map to operational management objectives (validation productivity, processing rate)

Description of Paper: Czvetko et al. (2021) developed a data-driven business process management (BPM) methodology integrated with Industry 4.0 technologies to redesign a CNC production line at a Hungarian assembly company. Using a real-world case study to transform a conventional manufacturing plant into a fully automated "smart" factory unit, the researchers identified key simulation parameters including processing times (CNC milling duration, operator-dependent variations), resource capacity (number of CNC machines, programmers, operators, cutting machines), arrival rates and scheduling requirements, operator utilization rates, and walking/transportation times. Three process improvement scenarios were tested through BPMN-based simulation: eliminating CAM program writing by operators, enabling operators to manage multiple CNC machines simultaneously, and introducing automated guided vehicles (AGVs) for material transport. The results demonstrated that Scenario 2 achieved a 40% increase in production capacity by reassigning resources more efficiently, while prediction models reduced estimation errors.

Description of Paper: Pereira et al. (2021) made a case study to improve the incident management (IM) process at a multinational company's IT support service. The researchers systematically analyzed the current process to identify five performance issues affecting processing time. Using simulation modeling, they tested four different redesign scenarios by applying specific BPM heuristics (activity elimination, activity automation, and integral technology). The analysis revealed that the optimal configuration—eliminating phone-based incident entry, automating all first-level support activities through system upgrade, and centralizing email as the single entry point—achieved a 10.7% reduction in second-level support processing time and eliminated 100% of first-level support processing time. This case study demonstrates how simulation parameters (activity automation, routing rules, system capabilities) directly correlate with management objectives (time reduction, error elimination).

Description of Paper: Braaksma et al. (2017) developed a reusable simulation model to evaluate implementing a combined walk-in and appointment system for CT-scan facilities. The study used discrete event simulation to test multiple scenarios at the Academic Medical Center in Amsterdam, examining performance indicators like access time, waiting time, and resource utilization. They systematically varied simulation parameters including the number of available scanners, appointment scheduling strategies, patient arrival rates, and walk-in tolerance levels to identify which parameter configurations best achieved management goals such as reducing patient access time from 4.7 days to under one day. The research demonstrates that simulation parameters directly drive performance outcomes and provides a practical methodology for translating operational objectives into specific parameter settings

Description of Paper: Al-Hawari et al. (2022) developed a framework to optimize educational dentistry clinics in Jordan. The study tested multiple simulation scenarios combining different parameters: appointment scheduling rules, orthodontist work schedules, receptionist staffing, and patient flow paths. They used design of experiments and their effects on performance measures (patient waiting times, length of stay, resource utilization, and throughput). Results showed that the optimal configuration reduced orthodontic patient waiting times by 37.74% and length of stay by 29.44%, while increasing patient throughput by 69.39%.
